Imperial Amnesia

An architecture of denial is the foundation of modern imperialism. And its primary building material is amnesia.

In the United States, in Britain, in every centre of imperial power that ever was, the history curriculum performs one function above all others, the erasure of empire from the minds of its own children.

This is not accidental. It is not an oversight driven by budget constraints or spending cuts. It is a deliberate, intergenerational project of scripted denial, based on the notion that if the memory is removed, it never happened. And if it never happened in the past how could anyone recognise it in the present.

The American high school student will learn their "Revolution." They will memorise passages from the Constitution. They will study the Civil War as a tragedy of brother against brother, a wound stitched together through national healing. They will leave school believing the moral arc of their nation bends inexorably towards justice. Because you can do that when you have painted every mass murder and genocide as an accident.

They don't learn about what US imperialists did in the Philippines. They'll never know that between 1899 and 1913, the United States military killed somewhere between two hundred thousand and one million Filipinos in a war of imperial pacification. Most Americans have never even heard about it so they get to live in blissful ignorance. A population was slaughtered so that Washington could prove to the European empires that it too could hold a colony. But the classrooms are silent on this and all imperial offenses.

They don't learn about the Banana Wars, decades of military intervention across Central America and the Caribbean to protect the fruit companies. They will not learn about Iran in 1953, where a democratically elected prime minister was overthrown because he wanted to nationalise his own country's oil. The CIA installed a Shah who ran a torture state, but the textbooks skip all that too.

They will not learn about Korea 1950 to the present day. Or Guatemala, 1954. Brazil, 1964. Chile, 1973. Argentina, 1976. Names reduced to dates, if they appear at all. The violence that has underwritten US power across an entire hemisphere is filed away as foreign policy trivia.

The reason for a redacted version of history isn't too complicated. A population that understands what was done in its name, across continents, across generations, would understand the word "freedom" very differently. When their president stands at the podium and announces yet another intervention to promote and defend democracy, a properly educated citizen would recognise something familiar in the presidential protestations. They would hear the spin and connect it to the spin of old.

History doesn't repeat itself but it rhymes. The excuses that corrupt politicians and captains of industry use to justify imperial misadventure don't change all that much over the centuries. If people knew about the past they would ask questions that press secretaries in the national security state couldn't sidestep or deflect.

This state orchestrated public ignorance has a lot of heavy lifting to do. Remove it, and the entire moral architecture of American exceptionalism becomes uninhabitable. The shining city on the hill is revealed as a garrison town. The land of the free and the home of the brave would stand exposed as an international arms dealer to torturers, supplying the instruments of terror to the world's true rogue states. The indispensable nation as the world's most consistent vector of violence and chaos... more

Written by Rory Mo-ran (Critical Theory)
